rows.evidence: Q1: section 'Farmers' rationale for using drip irrigation' - in-depth repeated interviews with 12 drip-adopting farmers in Bassi Tehsil, Jaipur District, in 2015 and 2016, plus review of GOI/GOR policy documents. Q2: same section - all 12 farmers reported no reduction in groundwater pumping time or schedules; farmers state they use about the same amount of water as under conventional irrigation or maybe more; Discussion - findings demonstrate rebound effect, drip leading to more rather than less groundwater use. Q4: same section - the intermediate pathway (intensification and expansion) is documented: irrigated share of holdings rose from ~40% to 67% on average after adoption, reduced row spacing, fertigation, greenhouses adding a third cropping season, shift to water-intensive chilies, and 4 of 12 farmers running solar wells by day and bore-wells by night. Q6: results are reported at the whole-farm level for 12 farms (holdings 1.38-6.33 ha, mean 3.7 ha), i.e., above the single plot. Q7: Abstract, Discussion and Conclusions - author states from the findings that in the absence of regulations over groundwater abstraction (and with subsidies/market incentives), drip is used to intensify rather than conserve water; promoting drip without groundwater-use rules is unlikely to save water.
rows.notes: Evidence is qualitative and self-reported (farmer interviews); no groundwater levels or pumped volumes are measured. Q3 no: single method (interviews); policy-document analysis does not bear on the water-use result. Q5 no: one tehsil, one region. Q6 'yes' is at farm scale only, not the state-wide scale the passage implies for Rajasthan. Q8 no: the paper notes that reliable state-level drip area data are unavailable but states no limitations of its own interview-based result. Q9 no: only averages and a range of landholdings, no dispersion for the water-use result.

rows.evidence: Q1: 'Farmers' rationale' section - repeated interviews with 12 drip-adopting farmers in Bassi Tehsil, Rajasthan, 2015-2016, and analysis of national and state groundwater/micro-irrigation policy. Q2: same section - farmers adopted drip to intensify and expand production, reported no reduction in pumping, and were aware their water demands were growing with negative impacts on groundwater; Discussion/Conclusions - in a regulatory vacuum (Rajasthan has no groundwater abstraction rules) drip adoption is exacerbating groundwater over-extraction. Q4: same section - intermediate pathway documented: irrigated share of holdings increased from ~40% to 67%, new water-intensive chili and greenhouse off-season crops, solar wells used to add pumping hours; one farmer reports earlier chili cultivation already depleted and hardened groundwater. Q6: results reported at whole-farm level across 12 farms (1.38-6.33 ha). Q7: Abstract, Discussion, Conclusions - the absence of groundwater-use regulations is stated as the condition under which drip leads to intensification and more extraction; drip without rules on groundwater use is unlikely to save water.
rows.notes: The function field is groundwater_recharge, but the study does not measure recharge or groundwater levels; its own evidence concerns farmers' reported pumping, irrigated area and crop choices (extraction side), matching the passage wording on excessive extraction. Q3 no: single qualitative method. Q5 no: one tehsil. Q8 no: no explicit limitation of the interview sample or method stated. Q9 no: no dispersion measures.

rows.evidence: Q1: 'Farmers' rationale' section - own field research, repeated interviews with 12 drip-irrigating farmers in Bassi Tehsil in 2015 and 2016. Q2: Discussion - the findings are presented as demonstrating the Jevons paradox/rebound effect: adoption of drip, a more technically efficient technology, leads to increased rather than decreased groundwater use; supported by all 12 farmers reporting no reduction in pumping and using the same or more water. Q4: 'Farmers' rationale' section - the mechanism of the rebound is documented: productivity gains (one farmer reports double production), irrigated share rising from ~40% to 67%, shorter fallows via greenhouses, shift to water-intensive crops, extra pumping with solar wells. Q6: farm-level results across 12 farms with holdings of 1.38-6.33 ha. Q7: Abstract, Discussion, Conclusions - the author states that the rebound occurs because of the absence of groundwater abstraction rules and a political economy incentivising intensification; without new institutional arrangements drip will not conserve water.
rows.notes: Study supports the rebound effect in one context only (one tehsil in Rajasthan), so the passage's 'observed in various contexts' is not supported by this study alone (Q5 no). Evidence is qualitative self-report, no measured water volumes. Q3 no: one method. Q8 no: no stated limitations of own result. Q9 no: no dispersion or uncertainty measures.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a qualitative political-ecology case study: purposive snowball sample of 12 drip adopters in Bassi Tehsil (nearly the whole adopter population at the time), interviewed in 2015 and 2016, combined with policy document analysis. No hydrological measurements; water-use outcomes rest on farmers' statements and reported changes in irrigated area and cropping. Author also offers a Jevons paradox interpretation drawing on literature, but the own finding is the interview evidence.
